title: The verse Gandhi would save
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: the Isha's first line, the verse Gandhi said could keep Hinduism alive
carry: the Lord lives in all this
tomorrow: half a verse, three moods. can you hear all three?

lines: GANDHI'S CHOICE: THE ISHA'S FIRST VERSE.
cards: Imagine every scripture of a religion burned, and you get to save one line. Gandhi said he knew which line he'd keep.
He told an audience that if all the Upanishads and every other Hindu scripture were turned to ashes, and only the first verse of the Isha survived in people's memory, Hinduism would still live.
Here's the line: isha vasyam idam sarvam yat kim cha jagatyam jagat. Back in year one it came in English. Today, in its own words, and one of them, vasyam, can be heard two ways.

teach.b: Start with isha. The stem is ish, the one who rules, the Lord, and this ending means by: by the Lord.
Then vasyam: to be dwelt in, or to be clothed.

teach.h: EITHER WAY: ALL THIS IS HIS.
teach.b: All this is to be dwelt in by the Lord. The world is a house with someone home. Every moving thing has the Lord living inside it, so nothing is empty and nothing is just stuff.
Here's the second voice, the one Shankara, the old commentator, takes. All this is to be clothed by the Lord.
Wrap everything in the Lord, the way you'd throw a shawl over a chair, so that when you look, you see the shawl first.

The rest of the line names what's being lived in, or wrapped: idam sarvam, all this, and yat kim cha jagatyam jagat, whatever moves in the moving world. Now the teaching, and why Gandhi would save it.
Either way you read vasyam, the Lord isn't off in a far heaven. All this is his.

That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, and many Hindus live it in small ways: touching a book that fell to the floor and then the forehead, bowing to a river, greeting the divine in another person with folded hands.

how: The Isha's opening line is one many Hindus learn by heart; small gestures, like touching a fallen book and then the forehead, treat ordinary things as belonging to the divine.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: the verse that says the Lord lives in all this
a modern summary of the Isha's main ideas
the Isha's verses as a hymn to Isha, a goddess

games.q: the first line, word by word — tap the pairs.
p: to be dwelt in, or clothed
whatever moves in the moving world

s: Gandhi said that if only the Isha's first verse survived, Hinduism would live
he named this one line as enough to carry the tradition.
Shankara reads the line as clothing all this with the Lord
a way of seeing: wrap everything in the Lord, and look.
isha is the name of the author of the Upanishad
isha means by the Lord; the text takes its name from that first word.

games.q: your study partner loves 'dwelt in': the Lord lives inside everything. you're asked to give the best case for 'clothed.' what do you say?
o: it turns the line into a practice: wrap all this in the Lord, then look.
it's the only meaning the word has, so 'dwelt in' is just a mistake.
it means the world is hidden from the Lord, so it has to be covered.
games.why: on Shankara's reading the line is a way of seeing: cover all this with the Lord, the way a shawl goes over a chair. both readings stay open in the Sanskrit.

practice: Say the line out loud, softly, one word to each slow out-breath: isha, vasyam, idam, sarvam, yat, kim, cha, jagatyam, jagat.
Then let the words go and listen to whatever moves: the breath, a sound outside, the next thought arriving.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, from its first word: isha, by the Lord, and vasyam, dwelt in or clothed. Two readings, one teaching: all this is his.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: isha vasyam, by the Lord, to be dwelt in or clothed, the Upanishad's first two words.

carryVoice: Your line: the Lord lives in all this. Gandhi would have saved that one line. Day one of the Isha, done.
